title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight - Space Radiation
summary: NASA lists space radiation as one of the five hazards of human spaceflight. It is invisible and considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

findings.text: NASA considers space radiation one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.
findings.quote: considered one of the most hazardous aspects of spaceflight.

limitations: The overview page gives no numbers, monitoring methods or countermeasures for radiation.

title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight - Isolation and Confinement
summary: Small groups confined in tight spaces for months or years may show behavioral responses. NASA says crews need careful selection, training and support.

findings.text: Crews must be carefully chosen, trained and supported for isolation and confinement.
findings.quote: Crews must be carefully chosen, trained, and supported

measurements: Behavioral responses in isolated crews are studied.
countermeasures: Careful crew selection, training, and support.
limitations: The overview page gives no numbers or unknowns for this hazard.

title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight - Distance from Earth
summary: The farther astronauts travel, the harder it is to get instructions, supplies and medical care from Earth. Self-sufficiency becomes essential.

findings.text: Mars is on average 140 million miles from Earth.
findings.quote: Mars is, on average, 140 million miles from Earth.

findings.text: Planning and self-sufficiency are key to deep space missions.
findings.quote: Planning and self-sufficiency will be key to successful deep space missions.

limitations: The overview page lists no specific unknowns.

title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight - Gravity Fields
summary: Bodies must adapt to changing gravity on the station, spacecraft, Moon, Mars and back on Earth. Muscles, bones, inner ear and organs all adjust.

findings.text: Mars gravity is three-eighths of Earth's, and astronauts could spend up to two years there.
findings.quote: three-eighths of Earth's gravitational pull for up to two years

measurements: Adjustment of muscles, bones, inner ear, and organs.
countermeasures: The page points to ground analogs, labs and the ISS as test beds for strategies; no specific countermeasure is named.
limitations: The page notes bodies will keep adjusting to new gravitational loads; no explicit unknowns listed.

title: 5 Hazards of Human Spaceflight - Hostile/Closed Environments
summary: A spacecraft is both a home and a machine, so its environment must be carefully maintained. NASA monitors microbes and immune responses.

findings.text: NASA monitors microbial communities and tracks immune responses in spacecraft environments.
findings.quote: monitoring microbial communities, and tracking immune responses

measurements: Microbial communities and immune responses are monitored.
countermeasures: Controlling temperature, pressure, lighting, and noise.
limitations: The overview page lists no specific unknowns.

title: Risk of Behavioral Changes and Psychiatric Disorders
summary: Long isolation and confinement in space can raise the chance of behavioral problems such as anxiety and depression. Long communication delays on a Mars trip add new challenges.

findings.text: Prolonged isolation and confinement can increase risk of behavioral issues.
findings.quote: prolonged isolation and confinement that astronauts face in space can increase risks of behavioral issues

findings.text: Communication delays on a multi-year Mars trip will create new challenges.
findings.quote: extended communication delays with a multi-year trip to Mars will create new challenges

findings.text: Windows can reduce monotony and boost mental health.
findings.quote: A spacecraft's windows can boost the mental health of astronauts because they reduce monotony

measurements: The page does not describe measurement methods; Earth-based isolation volunteers are studied over multiple months.
countermeasures: Self-care such as keeping a regular journal
Regular virtual contact with family and medical professionals
limitations: No quantitative data or effectiveness data for countermeasures.
How to support crew psychological health during long communication delays is still open.

title: Risk of Inadequate Teamwork
summary: Teamwork is a priority risk for deep space missions such as Mars. Communication delays, isolation and resource limits make team dynamics harder.

findings.text: Team dynamics and cohesion are vital to mission success.
findings.quote: Team dynamics and cohesion is vital to mission success.

findings.text: Risks include communication delays, isolation and resource constraints.
findings.quote: Examples include communication delays, increased isolation, and numerous resource constraints

findings.text: Earth-based simulations do not fully replicate spaceflight.
findings.quote: Though these simulations do not completely replicate the spaceflight experience

measurements: The page does not state what is measured or how.
limitations: The page gives no quantitative data.
Analog simulations do not completely replicate spaceflight (e.g. crews are not weightless).

title: Risk from Inadequate Sleep and Irregular Schedules
summary: Astronauts face sleep loss, irregular light-dark cycles and heavy workloads. These can cause short- and long-term health effects that affect mission success.

findings.text: The ISS has 16 sunrises and sunsets per day, which can disrupt the sleep-wake cycle.
findings.quote: 16 sunrises and sunsets per day

findings.text: LEDs that simulate Earth's light-dark cycle are used to help astronauts sleep better.
findings.quote: simulate Earth's light-dark cycle to help astronauts sleep better

measurements: The page does not state what is measured or how.
countermeasures: LEDs that simulate Earth's light-dark cycle
Research on light and caffeine effects on body clocks
limitations: No results reported from the light and caffeine research.
No sleep duration, quality or performance data given.

title: Risk of Inadequate Systems Operations Support
summary: On the ISS crews rely on real-time help from Mission Control when problems occur. On longer, more distant missions they must diagnose and repair systems on their own.

findings.text: NASA astronauts train on average 300 hours in simulators before launch.
findings.quote: NASA astronauts train, on average, 300 hours in simulators before launch

findings.text: Crews still rely on real-time assistance when problems arise.
findings.quote: crews still rely on real-time assistance when problems arise.

measurements: The page does not state what is measured or how.
countermeasures: Mission Control training on ISS systems
limitations: No data on how well crews perform without real-time support.
No required competency standard stated.

title: Risk of Injury from Dynamic Loads
summary: Astronauts face higher injury risk during vehicle landing due to gravity transitions, disorientation and bone loss. NASA builds human body models to understand these effects.

findings.text: Such injuries could significantly affect crew health and mission success.
findings.quote: Such injuries could significantly affect crew health and mission success.

findings.text: Crews on the Moon and Mars must self-egress and function autonomously shortly after landing.
findings.quote: crews will need to self-egress and function autonomously shortly after landing

measurements: Human body models characterize how the body is affected in spaceflight environments.
countermeasures: Research on crew readiness at landing
limitations: No quantitative injury thresholds or incidence rates.
Magnitude of bone and muscle weakening not given.

title: Risk of Radiation-Induced Cancers
summary: Astronauts are exposed to more radiation in space than on Earth, raising cancer risk and possibly other degenerative conditions. NASA studies prevention, health surveillance and personalized risk assessment.

findings.text: Astronauts are exposed to higher radiation levels in space than on Earth.
findings.quote: Astronauts are exposed to higher levels of radiation in space than on Earth

findings.text: Instruments aboard the ISS measure radiation exposure.
findings.quote: various instruments that measure radiation exposure are in place aboard the International Space Station

findings.text: Moon and Mars missions extend beyond Earth's protective bubble.
findings.quote: missions to the Moon and Mars will extend beyond this protective bubble

findings.text: Personal cancer risk assessments aim to use radiation dose and genetic factors.
findings.quote: based on radiation dose and genetic factors

measurements: Instruments on the ISS measure radiation exposure
Heavy-ion beams at the NASA Space Radiation Laboratory study effects on cells and tissue
countermeasures: Radiation shielding for Artemis and the lunar Gateway
limitations: No quantitative risk estimates or dose thresholds given.
Shielding needs for Mars and beyond are still being considered.

title: Ongoing HRP Research
summary: This page lists NASA Human Research Program studies on Artemis II, low Earth orbit and past investigations. Studies track crew well-being, immunity, and body changes in orbit.

findings.text: HRP uses research to develop methods to protect astronaut health and performance.
findings.quote: HRP uses research to develop methods to protect the health and performance of astronauts in space.

findings.text: ARCHeR monitored astronauts' well-being, activity and sleep patterns.
findings.quote: monitored astronauts' well-being, activity, and sleep patterns

measurements: Linked studies (21), all under https://www.nasa.gov/reference/ : archer, immune-biomarkers, artemis-ii-standard-measures, b-complex, brain-fluid-pressure, cipher, simulating-manual-piloting-for-moon-landings, spacecraft-occupant-protection, spinal-fluid-biomarkers, standard-measures, thigh-cuff, venous-haemostasis, zero-t2, omics-archive, tempus-pro; plus past investigations Altered Immunity, Food Acceptability, Food Physiology, Space Gardening, Spinal Health, Veggie Monitoring (nasa.gov/missions/station/ and nasa.gov/humans-in-space/ articles).
limitations: Page is an index; details are on the linked study pages.

title: ARCHeR
summary: ARCHeR tracks astronauts' well-being, activity, sleep and crew interactions during Artemis missions. It aims to show how hazards like isolation and radiation combine to affect performance.

findings.text: Data are collected with actigraphy and behavioral performance surveys before and after the mission.
findings.quote: Data will be collected using actigraphy and behavioral performance surveys before and after the mission.

findings.text: Actigraphy is also collected during the mission.
findings.quote: Actigraphy data will also be collected during the mission.

measurements: Actigraphy (wearable activity monitoring)
Behavioral performance surveys before and after the mission
countermeasures: Goal: develop protocols, interventions, and technologies (none named)
limitations: No sample size, results or metrics given.

title: Immune Biomarkers
summary: Starting with Artemis II, this study examines how spaceflight changes crew physiology including the immune system, using blood and saliva samples.

findings.text: The study aims to potentially counter spaceflight effects on the immune system.
findings.quote: potentially counter the effect of spaceflight on the immune system

findings.text: Details about dormant virus reactivation in space are still being explored.
findings.quote: details about this phenomenon are still being explored

measurements: Blood before and after the mission
Dry saliva blotted onto paper, collected in space and on Earth
Stress hormones, viruses and cells
limitations: No sample sizes or results given.
Dormant virus reactivation is still being explored.

title: Brain Fluid Pressure
summary: This flight study examines whether pressure of fluid inside the head is linked to eye and brain changes after long spaceflight (SANS). Fluid shifts in microgravity may raise intracranial pressure.

findings.text: Visual Impairment Intracranial Pressure Syndrome was identified in 2005.
findings.quote: was identified in 2005

measurements: Intracranial pressure
Eye pressure and neck vein pressure
Spinal fluid, blood and urine biomarkers, measured shortly after return and compared with preflight baselines
limitations: Whether spaceflight is associated with these changes is what the study tests.
Which biomarkers and which crew are at higher risk is unknown.

title: CIPHER
summary: CIPHER is a suite of 14 studies on how spaceflight affects the eyes, bones, heart and brain. Data are collected before, during and after missions up to a year.

findings.text: The suite has 14 studies.
findings.quote: This suite of 14 studies is designed to provide a better understanding

findings.text: Studies check whether bone and muscle loss changes after six months in space.
findings.quote: after six months in space

findings.text: Some studies collect samples on missions up to a year.
findings.quote: missions lasting up to a year will provide blood and urine samples

measurements: Blood and urine (calcium, joint biomarkers, telomeres)
MRI, CT and ultrasound of the heart and arteries
3D imaging of bones
Vision tests, vestibular tests
countermeasures: Resistive exercise studied for bone loss (as stated on page)
limitations: Whether bone/muscle loss accelerates after six months
Whether vision changes worsen with mission length
No results reported

title: Standard Measures
summary: This flight study collects a standard set of measurements across many body systems before, during and after spaceflight to inform protocols for Moon and Mars missions.

findings.text: Standardized measurements are collected across multiple body systems and time points.
findings.quote: This study collects a standardized set of measurements across multiple body systems and at various time points

findings.text: Activity and light exposure are gathered through a wrist sensor.
findings.quote: measurements of activity and light exposure (gathered through a wrist sensor)

findings.text: Saliva is used to measure immune function.
findings.quote: saliva to measure the function of the immune system

measurements: Wrist sensor for activity and light
Sleep reports
Fluid samples for diet and nutrition
Saliva for immune function
Cognition, sensorimotor and strength tests
Fecal samples for gut microbes
limitations: No sample sizes or results given; no unknowns explicitly listed.

title: Why do we conduct science experiments in space?
summary: ISS research prepares for deep-space missions and also helps health on Earth, for example for balance problems, osteoporosis, cardiovascular disorders and Type 2 diabetes.

findings.text: About 200 international experiments are on the ISS at any time.
findings.quote: On average, there are 200 international space experiments on board the ISS at any given time.

findings.text: Six months in space gives data that would take years on Earth.
findings.quote: Studying the human body in space for six months gives us data that would take years to gather on Earth.

measurements: Bones, heart, blood vessels and brain
countermeasures: Goal is to find countermeasures and treatments; none named.
limitations: No specific countermeasures or quantitative data given.
